papers.title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.

papers.title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
papers.abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

papers.title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.abstract: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.

papers.title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy
papers.abstract: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.

papers.title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
papers.abstract: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

papers.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
papers.abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

papers.title: ToolTurns: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Multi-Turn Dialogue
papers.abstract: Tool-using language models are increasingly deployed in conversational settings, yet most large-scale tool-use benchmarks focus on isolated requests. We introduce ToolTurns, a benchmark of 2,620 problems spanning 1,827 tools and 11,004 API endpoints across 47 categories. Each dialogue begins with an intentionally underspecified request and continues through two context-dependent follow-ups, testing clarification, tool use, and retention of conversational context. We also introduce an open-source user simulator that reveals withheld context through dialogue and generates follow-up requests, with a checker--fixer pipeline for improving its turns. Across nine language models, the best agent resolves 69.6% of individual requests but completes only 39.8% of full dialogues. Under this evaluation protocol, every evaluated model receives lower success scores on follow-up requests than on the initial request, and dialogue-quality rubric scores and task success can rank models very differently. Paired turn-level evaluation shows that the checker--fixer reduces detected dialogue defects, and blind human evaluation favors the revised turns. ToolTurns provides a testbed for evaluating whether agents sustain task success across multi-turn dialogue with tools.
